opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think there's a clean resolution. Zero data retention exists for good reasons. A lot of enterprise customers, and a lot of individual users, are sending sensitive material through these systems. If we want the models used in high-stakes settings, people need confidence that their data isn't being stored and pored over. But from a safety perspective, deployment is where you learn the most. You see the actual distribution of tasks, the weird edge cases, the ways models fail that you never anticipated in the lab.

So I'd break the response into a few pieces.

First, you can learn a lot without retaining raw transcripts. You can run classifiers or monitors in-flight on the traffic, have them emit aggregate statistics or flag categories of behaviour, and then throw away the underlying content. You lose detail, but you get signal on how often something happens and roughly what kind of thing it is. Designing those monitors well matters, because you only get the information you decided to ask for in advance.

Second, there's a big chunk of deployment that isn't zero retention. Consumer products, or customers who opt in, can give you much richer data under appropriate privacy protections. The risk is that this population isn't representative of where the high-stakes use is happening. The interesting agentic, enterprise, long-horizon stuff may be disproportionately in the zero-retention bucket. So you have to think about that selection effect and not over-generalise from what you can see.

Third, and this is where I'd push hardest, you should try to make your offline evaluations look much more like deployment. If you can't watch the real thing, build realistic environments, red-team aggressively, and use what you learn from aggregate monitoring to work out which scenarios you're under-testing. That loop between "we see a signal in the aggregate stats" and "we build an eval that reproduces it" is quite valuable.

Fourth, you can work out arrangements with customers themselves. Some organisations would be willing to run monitoring on their side, or share incident reports when something goes wrong, without handing over all their data. It's a bit like other safety-critical industries, where you have structured incident reporting rather than full surveillance.

The honest summary is that zero retention does make it harder to catch problems, particularly rare or subtle ones. I don't think the answer is to abandon it. I think the answer is to be clear about the blind spot, invest in privacy-preserving monitoring, and not assume that the absence of evidence from deployment means the absence of problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a real tension, and I think it's worth being honest that it's a tension rather than pretending it away. Zero data retention is a very reasonable thing for customers to want. If you're a law firm or a hospital or a government, you don't want your prompts sitting on a lab's servers, and I think labs should offer that. But the flip side is that a lot of what you'd want to know about how a model behaves in the wild lives exactly in that data you've promised not to keep.

So the first thing I'd say is you have to separate "learning from deployment" into a few different things, because they have very different data requirements.

One is learning about the distribution. What are people actually asking? What kinds of tasks show up, how long are the contexts, what tools are being called? For that you often don't need the content at all. You can compute aggregate statistics at inference time, before anything is discarded, and only retain the statistics. Things like classifier outputs, token counts, refusal rates, how often a particular category of task appears. You're keeping a histogram, not the conversations. There's a privacy engineering literature on this, differential privacy and so on, and I think labs are underusing it relative to how mature it is.

The second thing is learning about failures. This is the one I care most about from a safety point of view, and it's the hardest. If the model does something bad in a zero retention deployment, by construction you don't have the transcript. So you need mechanisms that fire in the moment. You can have monitors running alongside the model that flag a small number of interactions, and then the retention policy can carve out an exception for flagged cases with the customer's agreement. That's a negotiation, not a technical fact. Some customers will accept "you keep nothing except interactions your safety monitors flag, and here's the audit trail." Some won't. But I'd push hard for that carve out, because the alternative is flying blind on exactly the cases that matter.

The third thing is the customer themselves as a sensor. Zero retention doesn't mean the customer has no data, it means the lab doesn't. So you want really good channels for enterprises to report issues back, ideally with tooling that lets them share a redacted or synthetic version of what went wrong. And honestly, a lot of the most important deployment learnings I've seen came from a human somewhere saying "this was weird," not from automated collection.

And then the last thing, which is maybe the most important, is you shouldn't rely on deployment as your main source of evidence anyway. If your safety case depends on noticing problems after the model is in the hands of users, that's already a fairly weak safety case. You want the evals, the red teaming, the interpretability work, to be doing most of the load bearing before deployment. Deployment data should be the thing that tells you your pre deployment picture was wrong, not the thing that gives you the picture in the first place. So I'd actually frame the question slightly differently. Zero retention makes a bad strategy worse, and it's a good forcing function to not have that strategy.

The place I'd be most worried is the long tail. Rare, high stakes behaviour that you'd only see at scale. Aggregate statistics won't catch it, customers might not recognise it, and your pre deployment evals might not have anticipated it. I don't think anyone has a great answer there yet. The best I can offer is that the flagging carve out plus a very strong incident reporting culture gets you a lot further than people assume, and that we should be building the infrastructure for that now rather than discovering we need it after something goes wrong.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between retaining everyone’s conversations and having some way to learn when a model does something wrong. You don’t necessarily need the first to get the second.

For example, you can give users a way to explicitly share a problematic interaction. You can also test models in controlled settings, where the data is collected with permission, and use those failures to improve your evaluations. Those approaches won’t give you a complete picture of deployment, but they can give you useful evidence without routinely storing private conversations.

The difficult part is the failures people don’t notice or don’t report. If a model is very persuasive but wrong, the user may be perfectly happy with the interaction. So user feedback alone isn’t enough, and zero data retention does constrain your ability to investigate those cases.

I’d want us to be explicit about that limitation. Privacy is a real requirement, and learning about safety is a real requirement. The research question is how much useful safety information we can obtain with consent, or through carefully designed measurements that don’t expose the underlying conversation. And we shouldn’t assume we’ve solved that just because we have a thumbs-down button.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between retaining someone’s conversation and learning something about how the system behaves. You don’t necessarily need the former to do the latter. You could, for example, measure how often certain kinds of failures occur without keeping the underlying text. Or users could explicitly choose to share a particular interaction because something went wrong.

But there is a real limitation here: if you only collect statistics about failures you already know to look for, you’ll miss surprising new problems. So you’d want to combine that with testing in controlled settings, where you have permission to inspect what’s happening, and channels through which users can report unexpected behaviour.

I wouldn’t claim that completely recovers what you lose with zero data retention. The question is how much useful feedback you can preserve while respecting the privacy constraint, and which gaps you then need to address through other kinds of evaluation.
